title: AI Didn’t Replace Legal Judgment. It Exposed How Little We Teach It.
author: Olga V. Mack

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Judgment development: AI exposure is not professional readiness
st.an: Mack accepts the cluster’s distinction between AI exposure and professional readiness, expressly rejecting AI as a replacement for judgment. She materially extends the proposition through classroom-pilot evidence and a concrete instructional mechanism: AI-supported explanations can make reasoning visible, allowing schools and firms to teach judgment more explicitly, although the reported outcomes do not establish durable competence.
qs: The Product Law Hub pilot did not show that AI can replace judgment.
It happened because it made the reasoning process legible.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s human-led, work-redesign proposition and materially extends it into legal education and professional development. It argues that AI can diagnose weaknesses in how judgment is taught and that context-rich explanations can support judgment development, while its reported evidence primarily establishes engagement and completion rather than broad gains in professional competence.
qs: The difference in outcomes turned not on whether the AI provided the right answer, but on how it explained the answer.

kp.k: AI exposes gaps in judgment training
kp.d: The author’s central argument is that AI is not replacing lawyers’ judgment but revealing that legal education and law-firm training rely too heavily on judgment developing implicitly rather than being taught directly.
qs: AI is not replacing legal judgment. It is exposing how little of it we explicitly teach.
What emerged was not a story about automation. It was a story about instruction.
AI did not create that gap. It revealed it.

kp.d: The argument draws on Product Law Hub classroom pilots using Frankie, an AI-based legal coach, in a product counseling course. The stated evidence comprises quantitative engagement data and qualitative interviews, although the article provides no sample size, dates, numerical results, or comparative effect sizes.
qs: This became clear during a series of empirical classroom pilots run through Product Law Hub using an AI-based legal coach called Frankie.
The pilots were conducted in a product counseling course and designed to observe how students develop judgment-based legal skills when working alongside AI.
The findings draw on quantitative engagement data and qualitative interviews conducted throughout the course.

kp.d: The reported finding is that students learned more effectively when AI explained why legal analysis mattered to business decisions, stakeholders, and downstream consequences, rather than merely identifying a correct answer.
qs: The strongest learning gains occurred when the AI explained why an answer mattered in context, not simply whether it was correct.
When feedback connected legal analysis to business impact, stakeholder priorities, or downstream consequences, students retained more and engaged more deeply.
The difference in outcomes turned not on whether the AI provided the right answer, but on how it explained the answer.

kp.d: The article reports that product-decision context was associated with longer AI sessions and higher completion rates. Interviews also reportedly found greater student confidence in explaining reasoning, but the document does not quantify these outcomes.
qs: Quantitative data showed longer session times and higher completion rates when explanations tied legal issues to product decisions.
Interviews confirmed that students felt more confident explaining their reasoning, not just reaching conclusions.

kp.d: According to the reported comparison, feedback limited to correctness encouraged students to proceed quickly but did not help them explain an issue’s practical significance or communicate it effectively to non-lawyers.
qs: By contrast, when feedback stopped at correctness, learning stalled.
Students moved on quickly, but they struggled to articulate why an issue mattered or how it should be framed for a non-legal audience.
This distinction is easy to overlook because correctness is measurable. Judgment is not.

kp.d: The pilots reportedly showed consistent improvement in framing when AI modeled how to prioritize risks, explain tradeoffs, and tailor legal advice to product timelines, customers, and business strategy. The author attributes the improvement to making reasoning legible, not to superior AI intelligence.
qs: One of the most consistent improvements observed during the pilot was in framing.
Students became better at explaining tradeoffs, prioritizing risks, and tailoring advice to context when the AI modeled that behavior explicitly.
This did not happen because the AI was smarter than the students. It happened because it made the reasoning process legible.
It showed how legal considerations connect to product timelines, customer impact, and business strategy.

kp.k: Legal translation should be taught systematically
kp.d: The author argues that senior lawyers characteristically translate doctrine into practical advice, but this translation is seldom taught as an explicit process. AI can make this otherwise implicit professional reasoning visible to learners.
qs: In practice, this is what senior lawyers do instinctively. They do not recite doctrine. They translate it.
Yet that translation step is rarely taught systematically.
AI forced it into the open.

kp.k: Explicit reasoning may accelerate judgment formation
kp.d: The article challenges the professional belief that judgment can only be absorbed through experience. It reports that students improved fastest when shown the reasoning path and that their learning transferred across scenarios, supporting the author’s claim that explicit instruction can accelerate judgment development.
qs: There is a persistent belief in legal culture that judgment is something you absorb through experience, not something that can be taught directly.
Experience certainly matters. But the pilot suggests that judgment can be accelerated when it is made explicit.
Students improved fastest when the AI articulated the reasoning path, not just the destination.
That learning transferred across scenarios.

kp.k: AI supports judgment only under design conditions
kp.d: The claimed contribution of AI is conditional: it can support judgment development when designed to expose reasoning, context, and tradeoffs, rather than conceal the process or operate merely as an answer generator.
qs: Instead, the data suggests that AI can support judgment development when it is designed to surface reasoning rather than obscure it.
They require the same thing: support for reasoning, not shortcuts around it.
AI can help with that, but only if we stop using it as an answer machine.

kp.k: Educational dynamics may extend into legal practice
kp.d: The author says the classroom findings mirrored professional practice: contextual explanations promoted learning and credibility, while systems that removed nuance weakened trust. On that basis, the article argues that schools and firms share a need for reasoning-support tools rather than fundamentally different technologies.
qs: One of the more interesting aspects of the pilot was how closely classroom dynamics mirrored practice.
The same behaviors that supported learning also supported credibility.
Systems that explained context built trust. Systems that collapsed nuance undermined it.
This alignment matters because it challenges the idea that education and practice require fundamentally different tools.

kp.k: AI makes training deficiencies more observable
kp.d: The author contrasts immediate, observable AI interactions with earlier training practices in which senior lawyers compensated for junior shortcomings and feedback was uneven. This visibility is presented as exposing, rather than creating, deficiencies in professional formation.
qs: Before AI, gaps in judgment training were easier to hide.
Senior lawyers compensated. Juniors learned slowly. Feedback was uneven.
AI interactions, by contrast, are immediate and observable.
When a system explains why something matters, learning accelerates. When it does not, the absence is obvious.

kp.d: The article recommends that law schools and firms teach judgment explicitly by modeling reasoning, explaining tradeoffs, and connecting legal analysis to practical consequences. AI is positioned as an optional instructional aid rather than a substitute for human judgment.
qs: If we want lawyers who can exercise judgment, we have to teach judgment.
That means explaining tradeoffs, modeling reasoning, and connecting legal analysis to real-world consequences.
AI did not expose a weakness in lawyers. It exposed a weakness in how we train them.
That is a problem worth solving, with or without technology.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Mack argues that AI exposes shortcomings in explicit judgment training rather than replacing legal judgment, and can help develop judgment by making contextual reasoning visible.
pts.d: Olga V. Mack reports that students working with an AI legal coach learned more effectively when feedback explained business impact, stakeholder priorities and downstream consequences rather than merely identifying correct answers. She describes improvements in framing advice, prioritizing risks, explaining tradeoffs and tailoring advice to context, with learning transferring across scenarios. She further argues that immediate, observable AI interactions reveal gaps previously masked by senior lawyers' compensating efforts and uneven feedback. Extending the classroom findings to practice, Mack contends that context-sensitive explanations support trust and credibility, while collapsing nuance undermines them. Her framing is augmentation of human reasoning and training, not autonomous substitution for lawyers' judgment.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Mack grounds her claims in Product Law Hub classroom pilots using Frankie, drawing on engagement data, interviews and reported observations of student learning.
pts.d: The pilots took place in a product counseling course with realistic scenarios and AI support. Mack reports longer session times and higher completion rates when explanations linked legal issues to product decisions; qualitative interviews indicated greater confidence in explaining reasoning. She also reports improvements in framing and transfer across scenarios, but provides no numerical results, sample size, pilot dates, assessment instruments or detailed comparison design. Engagement metrics and interview-reported confidence are the specifically described evidence; retention, accelerated judgment development and transfer are reported findings without corresponding measurement details in the document. Implications for law-firm training and similarities with practice are Mack's extensions of the classroom account, rather than separately described workplace trial results.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source describes changes observed during classroom pilots and a conditional opportunity for legal training, without forecasting an adoption or replacement timeline.
pts.d: The article is identified as a 2026 publication, but does not date the pilots or specify their duration. Learning gains are described within the course and across its scenarios; no long-term follow-up period is stated. Mack makes the proposed benefit conditional on AI explicitly modeling reasoning, connecting analysis to real-world consequences and explaining why an answer matters. Correctness-only feedback is described as insufficient. She acknowledges that experience still matters and states that the pilot did not demonstrate replacement of judgment. The proposed application to firms and law schools has no specified implementation horizon.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The direct subjects are product counseling students; Mack draws implications for law schools, law-firm training and lawyers learning to communicate contextual advice.
pts.d: Students are reported to gain engagement, reasoning confidence and skills in framing tradeoffs and risks for non-legal audiences. Law schools and firms are presented as sharing a gap in explicit judgment instruction and an opportunity to use AI for reasoning support. Junior lawyers are implicated through the discussion of slow, implicit learning, while senior lawyers are described as traditionally compensating for training gaps and translating doctrine into practical advice. Product and business stakeholders feature as the context and intended audience for better advice, not as independently studied beneficiaries. The source does not specify firm size, market segment, staffing changes, client savings or access-to-justice effects.
